Unlike their Persian counterparts, Afghan divs are more closely tied to specific geographical landmarks — particular peaks, springs, and caves are known as div-dwellings. The folklore of Pashtun and Tajik communities includes stories of heroes who must outwit or overpower these divs to rescue captives or claim treasure. The divs of Afghan tradition reflect the harsh landscape they inhabit, embodying the dangers of the wilderness beyond village boundaries

name: Dokkaebi
description: Dokkaebi are legendary goblin-like creatures from Korean mythology and folklore, deeply embedded in both North and South Korean cultural traditions. Unlike ghosts (gwishin), dokkaebi are nature deities or spirits born from inanimate objects that have been imbued with spiritual energy over time — old discarded household tools like brooms, farming implements, or objects stained with human blood and emotions. They possess extraordinary supernatural powers and are known for their mischievous and unpredictable interactions with humans. Dokkaebi are neither purely good nor evil; they reward kindness and punish greed, often testing human morality through games and challenges. They are famously associated with the dokkaebi bangmangi, a magical club that can grant wishes and summon objects, though it cannot create life. Dokkaebi are skilled at ssireum (Korean wrestling) and cannot be beaten unless their right side is exploited. name: Doña Sebastiana
description: Doña Sebastiana is a folk figure from New Mexican Hispano culture, depicted as a skeleton riding a wooden cart or chariot, carrying a bow and arrow. She is the northern New Mexican variant of the Grim Reaper, brought by Spanish colonists and merged with Indigenous death imagery. Unlike the anonymous European Death, Doña Sebastiana has a name and personality — she is said to be vengeful toward sinners but merciful to the faithful. Her image appears in the santero tradition of New Mexican folk art, particularly in the bultos (wooden carvings) of the penitentes. In some stories, she is the same figure as Santa Muerte; snip in others, a separate entity — a skeletal woman who appears to those about to die, giving them a final chance to confess their sins. Her cart is said to be heard rattling through the mountain villages of northern New Mexico on the night before someone dies. Doña Sebastiana represents the unique religious synthesis of Spanish Catholicism and Puebloan spirituality that characterizes the Hispano culture of New Mexico, a tradition that has endured for over 400 years

name: Douen
description: The Domovoy, known as Domovoi or Domovik in various Slavic languages, is a household spirit deeply rooted in Slavic mythology across Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Poland, Serbia, and other Eastern European nations. name: Drac
description: The Douen, also spelled Dwen in Saint Lucian folklore, is a feared entity from Trinidadian and Tobagonian folklore with roots in African, French, Spanish, and English cultural influences. These are the spirits of unbaptized children who died before receiving Christian baptism, condemning them to wander the earth rather than finding peace in the afterlife. The Douen are most commonly found in dense forests and woodlands across Trinidad and the wider Caribbean, where they use their ability to mimic the voices of parents and loved ones to lure children away from safety and deep into the wilderness. Their primary purpose is to lead travelers and especially children astray until they become hopelessly lost, and they are considered one of the most dangerous folklore entities in the region, used by parents for generations to teach children the importance of staying close to home and the dangers of wandering alone

name: Drache
description: The Drac is a dragon-like creature from French folklore, particularly associated with the Provence region and southern France, where legends describe it as a shapeshifting water dragon that inhabits rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. Unlike the typical winged dragons of northern European tradition, the Drac is often depicted as wingless but possessing multiple legs, a long serpentine body, and the ability to transform into human form at will. In Provencal folklore, the Drac is known for its complex relationship with humans, sometimes demanding tribute from villages in the form of livestock or even human sacrifices, while at other times forming unexpected alliances with shepherds and farmers. The creature is deeply woven into the fabric of French medieval bestiaries and continues to appear in regional folklore throughout the country, where it represents the dangerous yet sometimes benevolent forces of nature that dwell in the waterways of the French countryside

name: Naga Berani (Dragon of Brunei Bay)
description: Naga Berani (The Brave Dragon) is a legendary sea dragon said to inhabit the waters of Brunei Bay, a large, sheltered bay on the northern coast of Borneo. According to Bruneian folklore, this massive naga was once a celestial guardian that descended to protect the waters of Brunei. Its serpentine body is said to be so long that it can coil around the entire bay, and its scales shimmer with the colors of the sunset reflecting off the water. The dragon controls the tides, protects fishermen from storms, and guides ships safely to harbor. In some tales, it is the guardian of a sunken kingdom beneath Brunei Bay — a once-great city that was swallowed by the sea as punishment for its inhabitants' arrogance. The dragon surfaces only during times of great significance for the nation, appearing as a line of shimmering waves or a mysterious wake in the bay's waters

In Greek mythological texts, the Drakaina appears as a sacred female serpent spirit that is typically slain only by gods or demigods rather than mortal heroes, reflecting her elevated status in the Greek mythological hierarchy. Notable examples of the Drakaina include Echidna, the mother of all monsters who mated with Typhon to produce Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, and the Nemean Lion; Campe, the guardian of the Tartarus prison who was slain by Zeus; and Delphyne, the serpent who guarded the umbilical cord of Zeus and was killed by Apollo.
